metadata.note: The Buffalo and Washington Railway -- a name far grander than what it built. Chartered to run south from Buffalo toward the Pennsylvania coal and oil fields and, in ambition, Washington, it got 14.40 miles to East Aurora in 1868 and another 4.80 to South Wales in 1870, and then renamed itself the Buffalo, New York and Philadelphia Railway in 1871. Under that name the line was finished in 1872 from Buffalo through Arcade, Franklinville and Olean to the Pennsylvania state line and on to Emporium, hauling coal, iron, oil and lumber north into Buffalo. Its corporate history is a procession of reorganizations -- BNY&P Railway 1872-1883, BNY&P Railroad 1883-1887, Western New York and Pennsylvania Railroad 1887-1895, WNY&P Railway 1895-1900 -- until the Pennsylvania Railroad took it over in 1900 and ran it as the Buffalo Line for sixty-eight years. Penn Central inherited it in 1968 and the last passenger train ran in 1971. The whole route is still in freight service under Norfolk Southern.
sources: https://nyrails.org/?page_id=5398 -- New York Railroad Archive, PRR Buffalo Line (the Buffalo and Washington Railway completed the 14.40-mile Buffalo-East Aurora portion in 1868 and built 2.32 miles of track in Buffalo; extended 4.8 miles to South Wales in 1870; renamed the Buffalo, New York and Philadelphia Railway in 1871 and completed the line from Buffalo through Olean to the Pennsylvania state line in 1872; owners in succession BNY&P Railway 1872-1883, BNY&P Railroad 1883-1887, Western New York and Pennsylvania Railroad 1887-1895, WNY&P Railway 1895-1900, Pennsylvania Railroad 1900-1968, Penn Central 1968-1976, Conrail 1976-1999, Norfolk Southern since; the line ran Buffalo to Emporium via Olean carrying coal, iron, oil and wood from Pennsylvania to Buffalo; about 23 stations including Buffalo, East Aurora, South Wales, Olean and Portville; the last passenger train ran in 1971 under Penn Central)

https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Data:Western_New_York_and_Pennsylvania_Railway.map (CC BY 4.0) -- used as the corridor guide only; its 'Buffalo and Washington Railway' feature measures 19.68 mi, matching the documented 19.20 miles the company built, which is what confirmed the extent of the company's own line
https://www.openstreetmap.org (ODbL) -- the drawn geometry, traced via Overpass along the surviving Norfolk Southern corridor
metadata.not_yet_sourced: Every headway and speed here is an estimate; no timetable has been consulted for any era. The 1971 end is given as a year, not a dated last train, and the source attributes it to Penn Central management without naming the train. The company's own name is inconsistent in the sources -- 'Buffalo and Washington Railroad' and 'Buffalo and Washington Railway' both appear, and the Commons map uses Railway, which is followed here. The charter date is not established, only that Buffalo-East Aurora opened in 1868. The 2.32 miles the company built inside Buffalo is documented but not drawn separately. The exact year the Buffalo and Washington name lapsed is 1871 per the source, but the second feature is drawn to 1872 so that the corridor does not blink out in the year between the renaming and the through line's completion; the 1871-1872 year therefore shows the company's built extent under the old name rather than the new one. Station lists beyond the five named stops are not sourced, and the intermediate opening dates between South Wales and Emporium are unknown -- the whole remainder is drawn as opening at once in 1872.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

properties.line: Buffalo and Washington: Buffalo – East Aurora
properties.speed_source: estimated: late-1860s steam on a new line up the Cazenovia and Buffalo Creek valleys; unsourced

segments.note: The Buffalo and Washington completed the first 14.40 miles of the line, Buffalo to East Aurora, in 1868, and also built 2.32 miles of track within Buffalo (not drawn separately here). The name looked south: the company meant to reach the Pennsylvania coal and oil country and, on paper, Washington. Frequency estimated/unsourced

properties.geometry_source: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap (ODbL): railway ways in the corridor were fetched from Overpass, filtered to those lying within 1.5 km of the coarse Commons route, and a shortest path run from the Buffalo end to Emporium. 1788 points, 119.09 mi. The Commons digitization (Data:Western New York and Pennsylvania Railway.map, CC BY 4.0) was used only as the corridor guide, not as the drawn geometry -- its median vertex spacing is 0.7-1.7 km with straight jumps up to 8.7 km, which is a waypoint sketch rather than an alignment.
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap, 199 points, median vertex spacing 60 m and 90th percentile 248 m; 4 of the 1787 steps exceed 1 km, all on straight tangent track. No leg is a drawn straight-line approximation. Traced 15.27 mi against the documented 14.40 miles Buffalo to East Aurora -- the traced line starts at the surviving junction about 3.7 km from the Buffalo terminal the mileage was measured from. The whole corridor is still active Norfolk Southern track, so the surviving alignment is what is drawn; where the 19th-century line has since been realigned that is not reflected.

segments.note: Extended 4.8 miles from East Aurora to South Wales in 1870, giving the company 19.20 miles of road. It renamed itself the Buffalo, New York and Philadelphia Railway in 1871, so the Buffalo and Washington name lasted only as far as South Wales; the years are carried to 1872 because that is when the through line opened and the successor feature takes over. segments.note: To Penn Central in the 1968 merger. The last passenger train over the Buffalo Line ran in 1971, under Penn Central management -- the year Amtrak took over intercity passenger service on May 1. Freight has continued ever since, to Conrail in 1976 and Norfolk Southern from 1999. Frequency estimated/unsourced
